title: Electrothermal behavior of superconducting nanowires buried in a commercial CMOS process
authors: Mohamed Gharib, Leonid Popryho, Salma Abdelzaher, Tejas Guruswamy, Tomas Polakovic, Umeshkumar Patel, Orlando Quaranta, Thomas Cecil, Clarence Chang, Yu-Sheng Chen, Thomas H. Swift, Grayson M. Noah, Alberto Gomez-Saiz, John J. L. Morton, M. Fernando Gonzalez-Zalba, Antonino Miceli, Inna Partin-Vaisband
abstract: Superconducting films native to a commercial CMOS process enable co-integration of superconducting devices (high-kinetic-inductance elements and nanowire detectors) with cryogenic CMOS on one monolithic die. Such films are buried in the front-end-of-line, beneath the back-end-of-line metal stack, an environment that might quench a self-heated hot spot. Current-voltage characteristics are reported for titanium nitride (TiN) nanowires in the polycrystalline-silicon resistor layer of a 22 nm FD-SOI process, and measured retrapping currents are compared with thermal models for longitudinal conduction to the contacts and interfacial phonon cooling into the stack. The wires are strongly hysteretic, with switching-to-retrapping current ratios I_sw/I_r of 7.4-9.8, sustaining a normal hot spot. For two wires of length ell = 50 micrometers and widths W = 0.50 and 1.00 micrometers, over bath temperatures T_b = 0.15-1.19 K, I_r follows the interfacial form (T_hs^n - T_b^n)^(1/2) with n = 4 (T_hs, the effective hot-spot temperature), and is strongly inconsistent with the (T_hs - T_b)^(1/2) constant-kappa longitudinal-conduction limit; free-exponent fits give n = approximately 4.8-5.0. An effective cooling coefficient Sigma_K = 7.9(3) W/(m^2 K^4) describes the data: 31(21) times below the acoustic- (diffuse-) mismatch value for a single clean interface, and approximately 12 times below the lowest previously reported comparable nanowire coefficient. The model-based film thermal conductivity is kappa = approximately 20 mW/(m K). Across lengths ell = 1-50 micrometers, I_r matches neither ell^(-1) of pure longitudinal conduction nor ell^0 of pure interfacial cooling; a two-channel model reproduces I_r(ell) with crossover length ell* = approximately 3.5 micrometers predicted, to an O(1) prefactor, from Sigma_K and kappa.
summary: This work characterizes the electrothermal response of superconducting nanowires embedded within a commercial CMOS chip. By measuring the retrapping current, the authors quantify the heat dissipation mechanisms, finding that the surrounding silicon stack severely limits heat removal compared to ideal interfaces. The results establish a two-channel model governing the current's dependence on wire length.
main_problem: The paper investigates the electrothermal behavior of superconducting nanowires integrated into a commercial CMOS process, specifically determining how heat is dissipated to sustain a resistive hot spot.
main_result: The measured effective cooling coefficient ($\Sigma_K$) is significantly lower than ideal theoretical benchmarks, indicating that the buried CMOS environment severely limits heat removal. The retrapping current ($I_r$) is governed by a two-channel model balancing longitudinal conduction and interfacial phonon cooling.
method: The study uses four-point I–V measurements across varying temperatures and geometries to compare measured retrapping currents ($I_r$) against theoretical thermal models.
model_or_system: The system is a TiN superconducting nanowire buried in the front-end-of-line of a 22 nm FD-SOI CMOS process. Heat loss is modeled via longitudinal conduction to contacts and interfacial phonon cooling into the surrounding silicon/metal stack.
key_observables: Retrapping current ($I_r$), switching-to-retrapping current ratio ($I_{sw}/I_r$), and the effective cooling coefficient ($\Sigma_K$).
important_parameters: Bath temperatures ($T_b$) ranging from 0.15 K to 1.19 K; wire widths ($W$) of 0.5 and 1.0 $\mu$m; crossover length ($\ell^*$) of $\approx 3.5 \mu$m.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting the temperature dependence of $I_r$ to an interfacial phonon radiation model ($n=4$) and employing a two-channel model to describe length dependence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hysteretic I-V curves, confirm the $T_b$ dependence of $I_r$ follows an $n=4$ law, and show the constant value of the extracted $\Sigma_K$ across different measurement points.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by characterizing the hysteretic I-V curves, fitting the temperature dependence of the retrapping current to determine the cooling mechanism, and finally analyzing the length dependence of $I_r$ using a two-channel model to extract the effective cooling coefficient $\Sigma_K$.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the detailed thermal modeling, phase transition analysis (superconducting transition), and non-equilibrium heat transfer mechanisms (phonon cooling) are highly relevant to understanding energy dissipation in nanoscale quantum devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Cross-section along the wire, not to scale. The TiN film lies on the shallow-trench-isolation (STI) oxide, is capped by doped polysilicon with silicide over the two con- tact ends, and is buried under the pre-metal dielectric (PMD), the BEOL metal levels (M1, M2), and inter-metal dielectric (IMD); isolated M1/M2 blocks are floating density fill, and dots mark where the stack continues. A hot spot at Ths loses heat along the film to the contacts (set by κ) and vertically into the surrounding layers (set by ΣK). ℓis the length be- tween the silicide pads; W runs into the page.

FIG. 2. Hysteretic current–voltage characteristics of TiN nanowires, ℓ= 50 µm, at Tb = 0.15 K. (a) W = 0.5 µm: the up-sweep switches at Isw = 1.055 µA and the down-sweep retraps at Ir = 0.109 µA. (b) W = 1.0 µm: Isw = 1.590 µA, Ir = 0.219 µA. Vertical dotted lines mark the extracted cur- rents. Each Isw above is that of the single trace shown; be- cause individual sweeps scatter downward through premature switching, the text instead quotes the maximum over the Tb ≤0.6 K plateau. Thresholds are taken on the positive branch; Ir agrees between polarities to within 4 %.

FIG. 3. Ir normalized to its 0.15 K value against Tb, for both ℓ= 50 µm devices, with Ir = C (T n hs −T n b )1/2 fitted in the prefactor C and the hot-spot temperature Ths and normal- ized at the same point, for n = 1 (constant-κ longitudinal- conduction limit), 2, and 4 (conventional interfacial phonon- radiation model). Among the fixed exponents shown, n = 4 best follows the data over the full range.
